# `env`

```bash
pnpm dist env check [--build] [--environment production|preview]
pnpm dist env setup [--environment production|preview] [--dry-run]
pnpm dist env rotate [variable...] [--yes] [--no-redeploy] [--dry-run]
pnpm dist env workflow
```

What a deployment needs in its environment, from what its apps declare: a
build that refuses to deploy without it and says exactly what to add, a setup
that adds it through the Vercel CLI, and a rotation of the secrets it
generated, with no downtime.

## Which deployments

A distribution with `apps/monolith` deploys it: one Vercel project, serving
every app, which has every app's variables. Without one, each app is a project
of its own, and each project has its own. A value two apps have to share — the
secret one signs in to the other with — is set alike in both.

Which project deploys what is kept in the distribution's `package.json`, so a
scheduled rotation in CI finds them without a `vercel link`. `setup` asks the
first time, and writes it down:

```json
"distribution": {
  "vercel": { "scope": "acme", "projects": { "apps/monolith": "acme-core" } }
}
```

## In the build

```bash
pnpm dist env check --build
```

`fg-dist init` runs it first, before anything is built, so a deployment missing
something fails in seconds rather than at its first request:

```
@acme/core-monolith is missing what a production deployment needs:

  FG_ID_SMTP_URL  (@fairgarden/id)
    The SMTP server sign-in codes are emailed through; without it, nobody can sign in by email.
    For example smtps://user:password@smtp.example.com:465
  FG_MEMBERS_SECRET  (@fairgarden/members)
    Encrypts the session cookie.
    A long random value: `pnpm dist env setup` makes one.

Add them to the Vercel project for Production, or run
`pnpm dist env setup` where the distribution is checked out, which adds them for you.
```

It checks on Vercel, for the environment being built — `production` or
`preview` — and nowhere else, unless `FG_ENV_CHECK=build`; `FG_ENV_CHECK=skip`
turns it off. It reads the environment files Next reads for a build, as
[`migrate`](/commands/migrate) does.

Without `--build`, it checks each deployment's Vercel project instead, through
the CLI.

## Setting it up

```bash
pnpm dist env setup
```

Adds what each project is missing, and nothing it has:

- A secret an app generates is made here, 32 random bytes, and set alike in
  every project that shares it — matching one already set, where one is.
- A value the app fixes is set as it says.
- Anything else is asked for, when there is someone to ask; otherwise it is
  listed, and setup fails.
- A database is not made here: connect Neon to the project, which sets
  `DATABASE_URL`.

`--environment preview` does the same for previews. Values go to the CLI on
standard input, never as arguments any other process could read.

## Rotating secrets

```bash
pnpm dist env rotate
```

Every generated secret an app marks rotatable holds a list, newest first, and
the app accepts all of it: it signs and sends with the first, and takes any.
Rotating puts a new value first and keeps the one before; the one before that
is dropped. So a session sealed, or a sign-in begun, just before a rotation
still works after it — until the next one.

A secret two apps share is rotated where it is checked first, and redeployed,
before what sends it: then there is no moment one side has a value the other
does not. In a monolith both apps read the one variable, so one redeploy does.
Production is redeployed after each step — the deployment serving it now, so an
instant rollback is kept, not undone.

Rotating keeps the current value, so a rotated secret is stored readable rather
than sensitive; everything else a secret is sensitive. Name variables to rotate
only those, and the ones tied to them.

Rotate less often than a session lasts is long, or people are signed out:
monthly is well clear of it.

```bash
pnpm dist env workflow
```

Writes `.github/workflows/rotate-secrets.yml`, which rotates on the 1st of every
month and on demand. It signs in to Vercel with `VERCEL_TOKEN`, an Actions
secret of the repository.

## What an app declares

Under `fairgarden.env` in its `package.json`:

```json
"FG_MEMBERS_SECRET": {
  "description": "Encrypts the session cookie.",
  "required": "deployed",
  "generate": "secret",
  "rotate": true
}
```

| | |
| --- | --- |
| `description` | what it is for, shown to whoever has to set it |
| `required` | `deployed` — any deployment — or `production` alone; otherwise optional |
| `sensitive` | a secret nobody should read back |
| `generate` | `secret`: `setup` makes it, and `rotate` can replace it |
| `rotate` | a list, newest first, that the app accepts all of |
| `value` | what it is set to; nothing to ask |
| `example` | shown when it is asked for |
| `unless` | not needed when any of these variables is set |
| `unlessMounted` | not needed when the app shares a monolith with this package: it works it out |
| `deployment` | the package whose deployment reads it, when that is not the app's own |
| `sameAs` | the same value as this other variable |
| `verifies` | it checks a shared secret, so it is rotated first |

`deployment` is how an app says what another needs to know about it: members
declares the variables the id service enrols it with, for the id service's
project — unless they share a monolith, where the id service works them out.

An app with [migrations](/commands/migrate) needs a database on any deployment,
without declaring it.
